title: Explain the execution flow of a parent task that spawns multiple child tasks and combines their results.
shortTitle: Explain the execution flow of a parent task that spawns multiple child tasks and combines their results

s1_definition.profdef: A parent task that spawns multiple child tasks is a fork-join or scatter-gather pattern: the parent splits work into independent child tasks, submits them to run concurrently, waits for all of them to finish, and then combines their individual results into a single aggregated result. In Java this is expressed with `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync` for each child, `CompletableFuture.allOf` to wait for all, and a combining step that joins the results, typically running on an `ExecutorService` thread pool.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh opens his portfolio dashboard at National Bank of India, the system needs three things: his account balance, his stock holdings value, and his mutual-fund value. Instead of fetching them one after another, the dashboard sends three runners out at the same time, one to each department. The dashboard waits at the door until all three runners return, then adds the numbers together into one total net worth figure. The three trips happen in parallel, so the dashboard loads in the time of the slowest single trip, not the sum of all three.
s1_definition.oneliner: The parent forks independent child tasks to run concurrently, waits for all of them, and gathers their results into one combined answer, so total time equals the slowest child, not the sum.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A parent task that spawns multiple child tasks is a fork-join or scatter-gather pattern: the parent splits work into independent child tasks, submits them to run concurrently, waits for all of them to finish, and then combines their individual results into a single aggregated result. In Java this is expressed with `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync` for each child, `CompletableFuture.allOf` to wait for all, and a combining step that joins the results, typically running on an `ExecutorService` thread pool.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh opens his portfolio dashboard at National Bank of India, the system needs three things: his account balance, his stock holdings value, and his mutual-fund value. Instead of fetching them one after another, the dashboard sends three runners out at the same time, one to each department. The dashboard waits at the door until all three runners return, then adds the numbers together into one total net worth figure. The three trips happen in parallel, so the dashboard loads in the time of the slowest single trip, not the sum of all three.

**One line to remember:** The parent forks independent child tasks to run concurrently, waits for all of them, and gathers their results into one combined answer, so total time equals the slowest child, not the sum.

sections.s2_technical:
The execution flow has four phases: split, fork, join, and combine. In the split phase the parent decides how to divide the work into independent units. Independence is essential, because if child tasks depend on each other you cannot run them concurrently. In banking a portfolio value naturally splits into account balance, equity holdings, and mutual-fund holdings, which are independent lookups.

In the fork phase the parent submits each child task to a thread pool so they run concurrently. With `CompletableFuture` you write `CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> cashF = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> accountService.getBalance(id), executor)`. This returns immediately with a future that will eventually hold the result; the actual work runs on an executor thread. You create one such future per child, and because `supplyAsync` does not block, all three are now running in parallel.

In the join phase the parent waits for every child to complete. The idiom is `CompletableFuture.allOf(cashF, equityF, fundF).join()`, where `allOf` returns a future that completes only when all the given futures complete, and `join` blocks until that happens. Crucially, the total wait time is the duration of the slowest child, not the sum, because they ran concurrently. You should always bound this wait with a timeout so one slow dependency cannot hang the whole request, for example `allOf(...).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`.

In the combine phase the parent reads each child's now-completed result and merges them. With `CompletableFuture` you call `cashF.join()` after the `allOf` has completed, which returns the value without blocking because it is already done, and then you add the three figures into a total. A cleaner compositional style uses `thenCombine`, where `cashF.thenCombine(equityF, (cash, equity) -> cash.add(equity))` produces a new future that combines two results, and you chain another `thenCombine` for the third.

Error handling is a senior concern. If any child fails, `allOf` completes exceptionally and the join throws, so you decide the policy: fail the whole aggregate, or degrade gracefully by substituting a default for the failed child using `exceptionally`, for example `equityF.exceptionally(ex -> BigDecimal.ZERO)` so a down equity service shows zero rather than failing the whole dashboard. You must also choose the executor deliberately: the common ForkJoinPool is fine for CPU-bound splitting, but for blocking I/O calls like database or remote service lookups you supply a dedicated bounded executor so you do not starve the shared pool. Finally, you must never block inside the executor threads in a way that causes deadlock, and you should propagate a correlation id into the child tasks for tracing. The classic alternative for CPU-bound recursive splitting is the ForkJoinPool with RecursiveTask, but for I/O fan-out across services `CompletableFuture` with a dedicated executor is the idiomatic choice.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Rajesh's net-worth dashboard at National Bank of India needs his cash balance, his equity holdings value, and his mutual-fund value, and fetching them one after another made the page take the sum of three slow calls. This is exactly the fork-join scatter-gather pattern, where we fire all three lookups concurrently so the page takes only the slowest single call.

Problem 2 — Occasionally the equity-pricing service is slow or down, and the old code failed the entire dashboard when any one source failed. This is exactly what per-child error handling with a fallback solves, so a failed equity lookup contributes zero and the rest of the net worth still displays.

Problem 3 — One hanging downstream once held the request open indefinitely. This is exactly why the join must be bounded by a timeout, so a slow child cannot hang the parent.

Our mini-project builds a portfolio aggregator. The code defines three services (`AccountService`, `EquityService`, `FundService`) each returning a `BigDecimal` after a simulated delay, a `PortfolioAggregator` parent task that forks three `CompletableFuture` children on a dedicated executor, waits with `allOf` and a timeout, applies a fallback to the equity child, and combines the three into a total net worth, and a demo that computes Rajesh's net worth and prints the per-source and combined figures.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: account SAV2001 (Rajesh); cash lookup takes 400ms, equity 600ms, funds 300ms.

Step 1: The parent `computeNetWorth` forks three `CompletableFuture` children with `supplyAsync` on the dedicated pool. All three start running immediately on separate threads; none blocks the others.

Step 2: The cash child runs on one thread, the equity child on another, and the funds child on a third, all at the same time. The equity child also has an `exceptionally` fallback attached so a failure would yield zero rather than break the aggregate.

Step 3: The parent calls `allOf(...).get(2, SECONDS)`, which blocks until all three children finish or two seconds elapse. Because they ran concurrently, this wait lasts about 600 milliseconds, the duration of the slowest child, not 1300 milliseconds.

Step 4: Once `allOf` completes, the parent calls `join` on each child. These return immediately because the results are already present: 1000000 cash, 450000 equity, 275000 funds.

Step 5: The parent combines the three into a `NetWorth` record and computes the total of 1725000. The dashboard receives one aggregated figure produced in the time of the slowest single call.

```
2026-10-24 14:12:30 INFO    child: fetching cash
2026-10-24 14:12:30 INFO    child: fetching equity
2026-10-24 14:12:30 INFO    child: fetching funds
2026-10-24 14:12:31 INFO    Cash   = Rs.1000000
2026-10-24 14:12:31 INFO    Equity = Rs.450000
2026-10-24 14:12:31 INFO    Funds  = Rs.275000
2026-10-24 14:12:31 INFO    TOTAL net worth = Rs.1725000 (computed in 612ms, parallel)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A parent task that spawns multiple child tasks and combines their results is the fork-join or scatter-gather pattern, and I describe its execution flow in four phases: split, fork, join, and combine. In the split phase the parent divides the work into genuinely independent units, because independence is what makes concurrency possible. In the fork phase it submits each child to a thread pool so they all start running at once. In the join phase it waits for every child to finish. In the combine phase it reads each child's result and merges them into one aggregated answer.

In Java I express this with CompletableFuture. I fork each child with supplyAsync on a dedicated executor, which returns immediately and runs the work on a pool thread, so after creating three such futures all three are running in parallel. I join with allOf, which produces a future that completes only when every child completes, and I call get with a timeout on it so one slow dependency cannot hang the request. Once allOf has completed I call join on each child, which no longer blocks because the results are already present, and I combine them. The single most important property is that the total wait time equals the duration of the slowest child, not the sum of all children, which is the entire reason for doing this concurrently.

The senior details I always mention are error handling and executor choice. If any child fails, allOf completes exceptionally and the join throws, so I decide a policy per child: either fail the whole aggregate or degrade gracefully by attaching an exceptionally fallback that substitutes a default. For blocking I/O children like database or remote calls I supply a dedicated bounded executor rather than using the shared ForkJoinPool, which is a bulkhead that prevents one feature from starving the whole application. I also propagate a correlation id into the children for tracing and always bound the join with a timeout.

On my project at National Bank of India, Rajesh's net-worth dashboard needed his cash balance, his equity holdings value, and his mutual-fund value, and the original code fetched them sequentially so the page took the sum of three slow calls. I rewrote it as a scatter-gather: three CompletableFutures forked on a dedicated pool, joined with allOf and a two-second timeout, combined into a net-worth total. The page now loads in the time of the slowest single source, and because I attached an exceptionally fallback to the equity child, when the equity-pricing service is down that source contributes zero and the rest of the net worth still displays instead of the whole dashboard failing.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that the parent forks independent child tasks with supplyAsync, joins them with allOf under a timeout, and combines their results, so the total latency is the slowest child rather than the sum, with per-child fallbacks and a dedicated executor making it resilient in production.
